connection: Production has models, repositories, repository interfaces, and clock-entry/employee services created in earlier sessions. Optional Side Lab 19B frames their public, private, protected, and internal declarations as dependency boundaries. App still constructs dependencies manually. Compose the production application with dependency injection and add PayrollService for the verified total-hours use case.
objectives: Explain why a class should depend on an interface, not a concrete implementation, when another class constructs it for it.
Trace how Program.cs's ServiceCollection registrations connect an interface to a concrete class at resolution time.
Read PayrollService's constructor as a real example of a declared-but-unused dependency, and explain why that is a legitimate (if incomplete) design rather than a bug.
Explain the real Transient/Singleton mix in Program.cs and what would change if every registration were Singleton.

visuals.title: The constructor states the contract
visuals.explanation: PayrollService's constructor lists IEmployeeService and IClockEntryRepository -- both required to construct the object, whether or not every method uses both.

visuals.title: DI resolves interfaces to concrete types
visuals.explanation: services.AddTransient<IClockEntryService, ClockEntryService>() is what lets the container hand back a working ClockEntryService whenever code asks for IClockEntryService.

visuals.title: Follow one resolution
visuals.explanation: provider.GetRequiredService<PayrollService>() walks the registration graph: PayrollService needs IEmployeeService and IClockEntryRepository, so the container builds those first.

visuals.title: Lifetime changes identity, not correctness
visuals.explanation: IClockEntryRepository is Singleton so every resolution shares the same in-memory list; IClockEntryService is Transient so each resolution is a new instance -- both work here because ClockEntryService itself holds no per-instance state.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does PayrollService's constructor take IEmployeeService even though CalculateTotalHours never calls it?
options: It is a real, documented dead dependency in the source app -- wired in for a future employee-lookup feature, not a mistake to silently delete
Every service in the app is required to take at least two dependencies
IEmployeeService is required by the C# compiler for constructor injection to work
preQuiz.explanation: decision-0006 in the source project's decision log confirms this was verified against the real constructor, not assumed -- the dependency is real and currently unused.

preQuiz.prompt: What does services.AddSingleton<IClockEntryRepository, ClockEntryRepository>() mean for two different classes that both request IClockEntryRepository?
options: They receive two independent repositories with separate in-memory lists
They receive the same repository instance, so entries saved through one are visible through the other
The registration is invalid because two classes cannot share one type
preQuiz.explanation: Singleton means one instance for the lifetime of the container -- this is why ClockIn and Clockout, resolved separately, still see the same _clockEntries list.

preQuiz.prompt: If IClockEntryService were registered AddSingleton instead of AddTransient, what would change in this app?
options: Nothing observable, since ClockEntryService holds no per-instance state of its own -- it only forwards to the (already-Singleton) repository
The app would fail to build
preQuiz.explanation: Lifetime only matters when a class holds state across calls; ClockEntryService is stateless itself, so Transient vs Singleton is a real but currently inert design choice -- exactly what decision-0005 documents and what Session 30 explores in depth.

concept.title: Depend on the interface, not the class
paragraphs: ClockEntryService's constructor takes IClockEntryRepository, not ClockEntryRepository. That one-word difference is what lets ClockEntryService be tested with a fake repository (Session 30) without ever touching the real one.

The same shape appears in PayrollService, which depends on IEmployeeService and IClockEntryRepository -- two interfaces, zero concrete types, even though CalculateTotalHours only actually calls one of them.

concept.title: Registration is where the interface meets its implementation
paragraphs: Nothing in ClockEntryService.cs or PayrollService.cs says which concrete class satisfies IClockEntryRepository. Program.cs's ServiceCollection is the one place that decision is made.

The real registrations mix lifetimes: IClockEntryRepository is Singleton, while IClockEntryService, PayrollService, and IEmployeeService are all Transient -- verified directly against the source Program.cs, not assumed.

concept.title: A declared dependency does not have to be used yet
paragraphs: PayrollService constructor-injects IEmployeeService but CalculateTotalHours never calls it. That is not dead code to delete reflexively -- it is a real, documented design point (decision-0006): the dependency was likely added in anticipation of an employee-lookup feature that has not been built yet.
The real xUnit test for PayrollService (Session 29) mocks IEmployeeService with Mock<IEmployeeService>() and never configures it -- proof, in the test itself, that the dependency is currently inert.

lab.objective: Compose the production application with dependency injection and add PayrollService for the verified total-hours use case.
lab.startingCondition: Production has models, repositories, repository interfaces, and clock-entry/employee services created in earlier sessions. App still constructs dependencies manually.
steps: Add the dependency-injection package to App if required.
Create PayrollService to total completed entry durations for one employee and period.
Register interfaces and concrete repositories/services with deliberate lifetimes.
Resolve the application services in Program.cs and run one complete clock-in/clock-out/total workflow.
Remove obsolete manual construction while preserving all prior production behavior.
lab.expectedBehavior: App composes existing production abstractions and prints total completed hours through PayrollService.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Implement the verified total-hours use case.
Keep the lesson synchronized with the cumulative build step.

review: The lab uses production because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: What would break if ClockEntryService's constructor took ClockEntryRepository instead of IClockEntryRepository?
options: Nothing at runtime, but Session 30's fake-repository tests could no longer substitute a test double
The app would fail to build immediately
postQuiz.explanation: Depending on the concrete type still compiles and runs -- the cost shows up later, when nothing but the learner solution can be substituted in a test.

postQuiz.prompt: Where in this codebase is the only place that names ClockEntryRepository as the implementation of IClockEntryRepository?
postQuiz.explanation: Every other file references the interface; only the composition root wires the interface to its concrete implementation.

postQuiz.prompt: Why is PayrollService's unused IEmployeeService dependency a legitimate design point rather than something to fix in this session?
options: decision-0006 documents it was verified against the real constructor and left in place deliberately for a not-yet-built feature
IEmployeeService cannot be removed from any constructor in C#
Unused dependencies always indicate a compiler bug
postQuiz.explanation: The source project's own decision log treats this as a resolved, intentional state -- not an open question to silently patch.

reflections: Which of PayrollService's two dependencies does CalculateTotalHours actually use, and what would have to change for it to use the other?
Why does IClockEntryRepository need to be Singleton for this console app's ClockIn/Clockout sequence to work at all?
What would you need to change if IEmployeeService's RenameService were later called from inside PayrollService?
whatBreaks: Changing ClockEntryService or PayrollService's constructors to depend on concrete classes removes the seam Session 30's test doubles rely on. Registering IClockEntryRepository as Transient breaks ClockIn/Clockout's shared state, since each resolution would get its own empty list. Removing IEmployeeService from PayrollService's constructor would break the real, existing xUnit test, which constructs PayrollService with two arguments.
summary: Constructor injection in this app means every domain class depends on interfaces, and Program.cs is the single place those interfaces are wired to concrete types. PayrollService's real, unused IEmployeeService dependency shows that a declared dependency does not have to be exercised yet to be a legitimate part of the constructor's contract.
